# Appendix {.unnumbered}

## 5-day rolling temperatures

The 5-day rolling temperatures showed marked temporal and spatial variability in Figure 5.1. The period from December to June generally exhibited higher temperatures, while the period from June to December was characterised by cooler temperatures. Northern Nigeria experienced more pronounced hot periods compared with central and southern Nigeria. Across the five-year period, temperatures recorded across all DHS clusters ranged from 14°C to 37°C.

![Five-day rolling mean temperature across DHS clusters, January 2020–December 2024. The figure shows the five-day rolling mean of daily 2-metre air temperature for all 1,380 DHS clusters from 1 January 2020 to 31 December 2024. The x-axis represents individual calendar days across the study period, while the y-axis represents DHS clusters arranged by latitude from southern to northern Nigeria. Each cell therefore represents the five-day rolling mean temperature for a specific cluster on a specific day.](images/tx5x.png)

## AFT model coefficients

Across the covariates shown in Figure 5.3, the magnitude of the ETRs appeared to be generally larger for the earlier antigens, particularly BCG and Pentavalent 1, than for the later antigens such as Vitamin A and MCV1. An ETR below 1 indicates a shorter estimated time to vaccination compared with the reference group, while an ETR above 1 indicates a longer estimated time. Compared with the North West, most geopolitical zones had ETRs below 1, indicating shorter estimated vaccination times, while North Central was generally closer to the reference. Mothers aged 20 years or older generally had shorter estimated times to vaccination than teenage mothers (≤19 years). Similarly, mothers with primary, secondary or higher education had shorter estimated vaccination times than mothers with no formal education. Children from the richer and richest wealth groups, and in some models the middle group, also generally had shorter vaccination times than those in the poorest group. Children delivered in health facilities had shorter estimated vaccination times than those delivered at home across the antigens. In contrast, the ETRs for birth order, residence and child's gender were generally close to 1, suggesting smaller differences in estimated vaccination time between their respective categories. Overall, the direction of the estimates was broadly consistent across antigens, although the magnitude of the associations varied.

![Exponentiated coefficients for covariates included in the adjusted Weibull accelerated failure time models. The figure presents the event time ratios (ETRs) for the covariates included in the adjusted models, excluding the heat exposure variables. The y-axis shows the covariates and their respective levels, while the x-axis shows the corresponding ETRs with 95% confidence intervals. An ETR greater than 1 indicates a longer time to vaccination relative to the reference category, while an ETR below 1 indicates a shorter time to vaccination. The figure is faceted by exposure measure, with the left panel showing the heatwave models and the right panel showing the heat index models. Estimates are coloured by antigen dataset.](images/covariate-forest-plot-01.png)

## Heatwave exposure sensitivity analysis

As expected (Pane 1, Figure 5.4), the proportion of children classified as exposed to a heatwave increased as the exposure window increased from 3 to 7 and 14 days. However, there was no clear pattern in the proportion exposed when different rolling temperature windows were used. The AFT estimates were also generally stable across the different specifications (Pane 2, Figure 5.4). For BCG, Pentavalent 1 and Pentavalent 2, all estimates, except one for Pentavalent 3, fell within the 95% confidence intervals from the main analysis. There was no clear or systematic change in the AFT estimates with changes in either the exposure window or the rolling temperature window. For Vitamin A, there was some indication that estimates were lower than 1 with the 3-day exposure window and moved towards the null as the exposure window increased to 7 and 14 days. A similar, although less pronounced, pattern was observed for MCV1. Overall, the results suggest that the main findings were not highly sensitive to the choice of exposure or rolling temperature window. Further research could examine the sensitivity of these findings to other methodological choices, particularly the choice of temperature data (maximum temperature data as opposed to mean temperatures used in our study), the return period used to define heatwaves, the choice of extreme-value model and the Weibull distributional assumption in the AFT model.
